column2: An electrically charged particle formed when an atom or molecule gains or loses electrons — chemistry's way of taking sides.
A small fruit tree or shrub bearing sweet dark berries, happily shared between gardeners and hungry birds.
A tiny glowing particle thrown off by fire or friction — often the modest beginning of a very big blaze.
One of the world's major monotheistic religions, founded on the teachings of the Quran and the Prophet Muhammad.
A sudden jolt of fear when your heart jumps slightly higher than the rest of you.
An aromatic perennial herb with blue or purple flowers, equally at home in the spice rack and the apothecary's jar.
The person who brings a case to court, armed with a grievance and a solicitor.
A genus of small flowering herbs, some of which have long earned their keep in traditional medicine.
The place where a river, stream or rumour first begins its journey.
The study of the human past — or simply everything that happened before you walked into the room.
The final result of a process or event, rarely known until the dust settles.
The final sum of a calculation or effort — the short answer to 'so, how did it go?'
A sturdy, long-eared domestic animal famous for hard work and refusing to rush for anyone.
Nerve pain radiating down the leg from the lower back — your spine's blunt reminder to lift with your knees.
An ancient Indian discipline of postures, breathing and meditation that proves how stiff you really are.
A chemical element vital for thyroid health, best known for staining fingers brown from a medicine-cabinet bottle.
The ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, famously used when someone doesn't care 'one' bit.
A sturdy wooden cask or barrel, traditionally used for salting cabbage, curing pickles or storing winter supplies.
The prominent lump at the front of the throat, particularly noticeable in men.
The state's funds and public purse — everybody's money, guarded by very serious accountants.
Capital punishment carried out by order of the state — a grim chapter of legal history.
An unusual incident or tricky legal case that forces lawyers to read the fine print twice.
A narrow decorative trim along the edge of a fabric, carpet or garden bed.
Pure, unbothered pleasure and relaxation — that rare moment when everything feels just right.
A traditional Russian ring-shaped or padlock-shaped wheat loaf with a handle you weren't meant to eat.
A vital mineral for nerves and muscles, famously championed by bananas everywhere.
An elegant ornamental plant with a funnel-shaped white spathe wrapping a central spike.
A carved relief portrait on stone or shell, or a brief celebrity appearance in a film.
A built-in hearth for a real fire, serving as a room's natural gathering spot on cold evenings.
A tall, hollow-stemmed wetland grass forming dense green walls along rivers and lakes.
A waterway dug for ships, or the frequency bringing news and television into your living room.
The tailored upper half of a suit, capable of making even a T-shirt look faintly respectable.
A thick, heavy cord of twisted fibres trusted by sailors, climbers and tug-of-war teams.
A coarse, open-weave fabric used as the grid for embroidery or stretched onto a painter's frame.
An established rule, standard or body of classic works against which everything else is measured.
The commander of a ship or aircraft, or the player in charge of keeping a sports team from arguing.
A tiny sphere of liquid held together by surface tension — the minimum dose of rain.
An old-fashioned women's hat tied neatly under the chin, framing the face.
Severe punishment or vengeance handed down for a wrongdoing, often with dramatic flair.
A unit of weight for gemstones equal to 0.2 grams — a tiny measure for very expensive habits.
A large freshwater fish of ponds and rivers, prized by anglers and festive dinner tables alike.
A landscape of sinkholes, caves and underground streams carved out by water dissolving limestone.
A flat diagram of the world, or one of fifty-two cards deciding your luck on Friday night.
A tough protective headgear worn by builders, soldiers and cyclists anticipating trouble.
A rigid, hereditary social group into which one is born, with very little room for moving up.
Inflammation of the mucous membranes accompanied by excessive mucus — a decidedly unglamorous medical term.
A small motorboat built for harbour trips, river outings or ferrying passengers ashore.
Either of the two shorter sides forming the right angle in a right-angled triangle.
The electrode where reduction occurs in an electrochemical cell — famously confused with its opposite in physics exams.
A heavy construction machine for flattening tarmac, or an ice rink for people on blades.
A private room aboard a ship where the ocean is right outside your porthole.
A narrow, covered canoe propelled with a double-bladed paddle, built for rapids and calm lakes alike.
The smallest discrete packet of energy in physics — microscopic in size, colossal in consequences.
An elementary particle that teams up to form protons and neutrons — one of matter's tiniest building blocks.
An official limit or fixed share allocated for imports, production or participation.
The measurement of a font's height in typography, deciding whether a contract is readable or requires a magnifying glass.
A wooden or plastic pin set up at the end of a lane, waiting to be knocked flying by a heavy ball.
An evergreen conifer prized for its fragrant wood, longevity and majestic silhouette.
A sweet baked treat studded with raisins or nuts, practically mandatory alongside an afternoon cup of tea.
A member of the ancient or modern peoples of Ireland, Scotland, Wales and Brittany.
A small, austere room where a monk lives in quiet prayer and contemplation.
A tangy, probiotic fermented milk drink made with live kefir grains.
A tall, cylindrical military dress cap with a visor and plume, popular in 19th-century armies.
A brief downward tilt of the head meaning 'yes', 'hello' or 'I'm pretending to listen'.
A shrub or small tree bearing tart red berries, ideal for jams, compotes and savoury sauces.
A long, tapered wooden stick used to strike balls in billiards, snooker or pool.
The central lengthwise timber or steel beam along the bottom of a ship's hull — its structural backbone.
A pungent culinary herb that ruthlessly divides dinner guests into lovers and soap-tasting haters.
A tiny street booth or pavilion selling newspapers, snacks or coffee where a full shop wouldn't fit.
A Lutheran or Protestant church, particularly in German- or Scots-speaking traditions.
A small drawstring bag traditionally used for carrying loose tobacco or coins.
An ultra-fine, sheer cotton fabric that barely conceals whatever lies behind it.
A closed sac of fluid or tissue in the body that calls for a doctor rather than a guess.
The grasping part of the arm below the wrist, or a brush used by an artist.
The largest mammal on Earth — an ocean giant that breathes air and sings across miles of sea.
The long, winding tube of the digestive tract quietly extracting energy from last night's dinner.
An array of buttons for typing text, serving as the frontline between your fingers and typos.
Hidden gold, jewels or ancient artefacts worth digging up the back garden for.
A tight-knit family or social group bound by shared ancestry, loyalty and inside jokes.
The long-awaited tug on a fishing line when the float finally stops just decorating the water.
An adhesive meant to bond broken things together — though it mostly prefers bonding your fingers.
A deciduous tree famous for its palm-shaped leaves, fiery autumn colours and pancake-friendly syrup.
A trouser leg or skirt that widens dramatically below the knee, straight out of the 1970s.
A tiny parasitic arachnid waiting patiently in long grass to hitch a ride on hikers and dogs.
A crisp tap of a mouse button — the smallest physical effort required to buy something online.
A tapered block driven into a gap to split wood, hold a door open or prop up a wobbly table.
A short video segment, often accompanying a song or capturing five seconds of internet fame.
A loud rallying call or shout meant to summon a crowd or lift spirits.
An organism or cell genetically identical to its parent, produced by nature or a laboratory.
A tiny, nocturnal blood-feeding insect and the ultimate nightmare guest in any mattress.
A circus performer in greasepaint and oversized shoes dedicated to slapstick and chaos.
A long, pointed canine tooth built for gripping prey or starring in vampire films.
The horny jaws of a bird, serving simultaneously as mouth, tweezers, nutcracker and toolkit.
A hooked walking stick used for support — and a classic accessory for fairy-tale elders.
A sturdy post on a ship's deck or quayside around which heavy mooring ropes are secured.
Bound pages of text and pictures — a portable time machine requiring neither Wi-Fi nor a charger.
A flexible lash attached to a handle, historically used to drive horses or enforce harsh discipline.
A venomous snake famous for flaring its dramatic neck hood when feeling threatened.
A woven floor covering that adds warmth to a room while quietly collecting crumbs and pet hair.
Shaping red-hot metal with heavy hammer blows on an anvil until iron obeys.
A system of secret symbols, or the instructions that tell a computer what to do next.
The concluding passage of a piece of music, bringing the whole performance to a neat close.
The body's largest organ and outer protective wrapper, meeting the elements first.
A protective outer shell housing machinery or wiring, keeping dust and curious fingers out.
A secret, underhand plot or scheming manoeuvre that rarely ends well for anyone.
A narrow, no-frills bed found in barracks, dormitories, hospitals or ships' cabins.
A clever, adaptable wild canine of North America, famous for howling at dusk.
A silky protective case spun by a caterpillar before its dramatic wardrobe change into a butterfly.
A large tropical palm fruit with a fibrous husk, hard shell and built-in refreshing drink.
A high-carbon solid fuel baked from coal, essential for smelting iron in blast furnaces.
A sharpened wooden post driven into the ground for fencing — or hunting vampires.
A dark, fizzy, caffeinated soft drink instantly recognisable anywhere in the world.
A glass laboratory vessel with a narrow neck and wide body, built for swirling chemical experiments.
A deep track worn into a dirt road by passing wheels — easy to fall into, hard to steer out of.
Inflammation of the inner lining of the colon, best left to a gastroenterologist rather than guesswork.
The grain-bearing tip of a wheat or barley stalk where the harvest takes shape.
The German philosopher who wrote about Zarathustra and warned against staring too long into the abyss.
The spiritual title of Siddhartha Gautama, the sage whose awakening founded a major world religion.
An ancient Indian religion and philosophy based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama.
A dramatic surge in vibration amplitude when an external frequency matches a system's natural rhythm.
The English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction and gave his name to a protective cage.
The ancient Chinese philosopher traditionally credited with founding Taoism.
The 14th-century Turco-Mongol conqueror who built the Timurid Empire from his capital in Samarkand.
The cigar-smoking British statesman, writer and wartime Prime Minister who led the UK through WWII.
The chemical element at the heart of modern microchips, computers and beach sand.
A heavy splitting maul with a simple philosophy: if a log refuses to share, persuade it by force.
The iconic revolver synonymous with the American Wild West — a cowboy feels underdressed without one.
A tiny, high-pitched bloodsucker capable of ruining the sleep of a creature ten thousand times its size.
A performer paid to make strangers laugh — doing professionally what everyone else tries for free in the family group chat.
A low bedroom cabinet with sliding drawers that stores socks, paperwork and the mystery of the missing glove.
A small, dense clump of dough, paper or wool — roughly matching the shape of Monday morning's to-do list.
An electronic marvel capable of guiding rockets to Mars, yet baffled when you accidentally click the wrong button.
The starting line of a game, or the opening stake placed on the table before cards are dealt.
The final chapter or closing credits — the moment even the longest TV series finally has to say goodbye.
A 19th-century streetcar pulled along iron rails by horses working a regular shift.
A massive continuous expanse of land surrounded by oceans — real estate on a planetary scale.
A geometric shape with a circular base tapering to a single point, looking like a party hat for a strict triangle.
A stable worker who tends to horses and knows far more about equine moods than human ones.
An office machine that reproduces documents faster than office gossip spreads.
A faithful reproduction of an original — occasionally turning out neater than the first attempt.
A large mound of dried grass piled in a field — a rustic mattress, though notoriously tricky for finding needles.
A flat baked disc of cake or pastry forming the edible foundation for cream, jam and icing.
The crisp, browned outer shell of a loaf or cheese wedge — frequently the subject of household negotiations.
Food for pets or livestock that vanishes from the bowl faster than you can say 'bon appétit'.
A rigid rectangular container — the humble ancestor of modern packaging, lid optional.
A marked rectangular arena where tennis players bat a yellow ball back and forth while pretending to stay calm.
A contagious viral illness marked by fever and a red rash, now largely kept at bay by routine vaccination.
A brew of roasted, ground beans that acts as morning's chief diplomat, persuading humans to become human.
A member of an indigenous people of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, famed for reindeer herding and coastal life.
A farmhand wielding a scythe to cut grass or grain, leaving the meadow neater than a fresh haircut.
The rigid living tissue of the skeleton — internal scaffolding keeping us from collapsing into a puddle.
A male domestic cat who firmly believes he owns the flat and merely employs you as staff.
A large heated vessel or industrial tank tasked with warming water and radiators for an entire building.
A knitted top with sleeves that emerges from the wardrobe the moment someone says, 'Is it chilly in here?'
A tightly packed globe of cabbage or lettuce leaves that requires zero supermarket plastic wrap.
A small, grassy mound rising out of a marsh — nature's stepping stone designed to soak your boots.
A sleek, independent feline ruler of the household with a lifelong devotion to empty cardboard boxes.
A thick, dense matted wool blanket tough enough to insulate yurts or smother flames.
An immortal Slavic fairy-tale villain who hid his soul inside a needle, an egg, a duck and a hare — the pioneer of two-factor authentication.
A clawed marine crustacean that navigates life's challenges by walking strictly sideways.
The unlawful taking of someone else's property — shopping with a 100% discount and terrible legal prospects.
The outer border of an object, table or cliff where one thing ends and thin air begins.
A valve controlling the flow of water or gas — a small metal handle holding immense power over your mood.
Tiny dots or flecks of a contrasting colour scattered across a surface like accidental paint splashes.
Visual charm and elegance — an old-fashioned word that sounds dressier than an everyday compliment.
The total failure of a plan, business or system when a grand idea meets reality and loses.
A smooth, rich emulsion applied either to dry skin or generously between layers of cake.
The sideways tilt of a ship in rough water when the horizon suddenly refuses to stay level.
A person of mixed European and African or Indigenous heritage, or a language born from cultural crossroads.
A lightweight fabric with a crisp, pebbled texture — or a very thin French pancake, depending on lunchtime.
Two intersecting lines forming an ancient geometric figure and one of the world's most recognised symbols.
A sudden turning point or emergency when everything demands immediate repair.
A loud, piercing vocal outburst guaranteed to be heard by everyone who ignored your normal voice.
Tiny shrimp-like marine crustaceans forming the bulk of a blue whale's daily takeaway.
A roof overhead that protects you from the elements — most appreciated when rain arrives uninvited.
The red liquid circulating through veins and arteries — the body's 24/7 courier service.
The pattern and shaping of fabric pieces on a tailor's table before a single seam is sewn.
A long-distance race across fields, mud and hills where tarmac was never invited.
A velvety subterranean mammal with shovel-like paws that digs tunnels without a hard hat or planning permission.
A round geometric shape with every point equidistant from the centre — zero corners and a compass's favourite subject.
A holiday aboard a floating resort where your hotel politely moves to a new city while you sleep.
Hulled cereal grains like buckwheat or oats — tiny pellets that magically triple in size inside a saucepan.
A steep, high riverbank or cliff where admiring the view requires watching your step.
The feathered limb of a bird or the aerofoil of a plane that makes gravity negotiable.
The top covering of a building — essentially a giant umbrella that refuses to fold up.
An ornamental cup awarded to a champion — strictly for hoisting overhead, not drinking tea from.
The child of your aunt or uncle — the family member sharing the same branch of the family tree.
A small rolled paper funnel once used by shopkeepers to weigh out sweets and sunflower seeds.
A long-legged wading bird that patrols shorelines and marshes poking the mud for lunch.
A bedroom cabinet with drawers — and occasionally a hinged writing flap for bills you're avoiding.
A tall, narrow chest of drawers that stores socks, paperwork and the mystery of the missing glove.
Devoted veneration of a leader, object or idea — when admiration forgets where the brakes are.
The shared arts, customs, beliefs and achievements that separate civilisation from a random crowd.
A man who sponsors a child at baptism — often doubling as a lifelong family friend and festive guest.
A woman who sponsors a child at baptism, bound to the family by ritual, affection and birthday gifts.
A bright red cotton fabric historically favoured for traditional Slavic dress and revolutionary banners.
A statue worshipped as a deity, or a celebrity whose posters outnumber family photos on a teenager's wall.
A mildly alcoholic fermented drink made from mare's milk, beloved across the Central Asian steppes.
A sworn friend and trusted guest in the traditions of the Caucasus mountains.
The art of mixing different wines, teas or whiskies to create a harmony none could achieve alone.
A trader or business owner of old, for whom the bustling market square was the boardroom.
The act of buying goods for money — the half of a transaction where your wallet gets lighter.
A rounded, hemispherical roof crowning a cathedral, observatory or capitol building.
A detachable voucher promising a discount or freebie before its tiny expiry date runs out.
The small curved lever squeezed to fire a gun — or anything that sets off an immediate reaction.
A direction of travel, a series of lectures, or today's exchange rate.
A separated portion of a whole — vanishing twice as fast when it's the last slice of cake.
A woody perennial plant with multiple stems — greener than a weed, more modest than a tree.
A wild, noisy bout of partying and overindulgence that leaves morning-after regret.
The room where meals are cooked and guests inevitably congregate during every house party.
A messy, unorganised pile of stuff — the universal filing system right up until tidying day.
The driver of a horse-drawn carriage, steering with leather reins instead of power steering.
A massive windfall or gambling prize — the dream that keeps players pushing chips onto the table.
A wide decorative cloth belt wrapped around a traditional coat to hold both garment and posture together.
A shady, leafy shelter woven from branches and foliage — nature's temporary summerhouse.
A member of Cambodia's predominant ethnic group, heirs to the ancient builders of Angkor Wat.
A drainage trench dug alongside a road to catch rainwater and overly ambitious winter drivers.
A unit of radioactivity named after Marie and Pierre Curie — best admired from behind lead shielding.
A soft, thin unleavened flatbread from the Caucasus and Middle East — the ultimate edible wrap.
An aromatic evergreen tree whose leaves crown both Olympic victors and a good pot of soup.
An aromatic tree resin burned in censers to give churches their unmistakable solemn scent.
A focused beam of coherent light capable of reading discs, cutting steel and driving cats mad.
The sharp vocal sound made by a dog — a brief message rarely requiring translation.
A liveried household servant of grand estates, trained in impeccable bows and zero personal free time.
A device housing a bulb or flame — a miniature domestic sun controlled by a flick of a switch.
A graceful woodland deer sporting white-spotted summer coats like natural camouflage.
The padded, clawed foot of a cat, dog or bear — ideal for running, climbing and knocking mugs off tables.
A traditional Russian bat-and-ball team game where hitting the ball means sprinting for your life.
A large wooden storage box or market bin packed tighter than an airline carry-on bag.
A crisp leafy green vegetable that makes any dinner plate look instantly healthier before the first bite.
The wheeled frame supporting an artillery cannon so it can be aimed and rolled into battle.
Someone who deliberately bends the truth — an author of creative fiction who struggles to remember previous chapters.
A strutting male chicken with a red comb and a built-in dawn alarm lacking a snooze button.
Frozen water — a transparent surface specifically engineered to test the balance of confident pedestrians.
A safety rope or cable rigged along a ship's deck to keep sailors from becoming involuntary swimmers.
A heavily reinforced ship built to smash straight through frozen seas instead of waiting for spring.
A wide-eyed, long-tailed primate native to Madagascar with a permanently surprised expression.
A blue-flowered crop whose fibres weave fine linen and whose seeds yield nutritious oil.
A narrow strip of fabric or paper used for wrapping parcels, tying hair or pinning on medals.
The adorable, incomprehensible chatter of toddlers whose thoughts move faster than their diction.
Shaping clay, wax or plasticine by hand to turn imagination into something you can put on a shelf.
A modest charitable donation or small contribution — famous from a biblical widow's generous offering.
A vast expanse of trees and undergrowth where mushrooms always know the way better than hikers.
A nearly invisible nylon thread connecting a hopeful angler to whatever is lurking beneath the surface.
The liverpudlian singer, songwriter and rhythm guitarist who co-founded The Beatles and imagined peace.
The reclusive American author who gave the world Holden Caulfield in 'The Catcher in the Rye'.
A tiny nocturnal primate of Southeast Asia whose enormous eyes are each heavier than its brain.
A tall, dome-shaped Italian sweet bread studded with candied fruit and raisins that conquers British supermarkets every December.
A traditional British Easter fruitcake topped with toasted marzipan and eleven little almond paste balls.
A traditional German Christmas fruit loaf dusted with icing sugar and hiding a sweet seam of marzipan inside.
